description: Without bees, **75% of the world's food crops** would be at risk. These quiet little workers hold up our food supply, and their populations are collapsing.

hero.hook: They do more than make honey: without them, a large part of our food would disappear.

blocks.text: We usually think of bees only for their honey. In truth they provide a far bigger service: they let most flowering plants reproduce. That service is worth hundreds of billions of dollars every year.

Over the past few decades, these essential insects have been vanishing at a worrying speed. Understanding their role, and the causes of their decline, makes clear how directly our future food supply is at stake.

In simple terms, [[pollination]] is the transport of pollen, the male cells of a flower, to the female organ of another flower of the same species. Wind and water can sometimes do the job, but most flowering plants prefer an animal courier. While gathering nectar and pollen for their colony, bees carry out that transport without knowing it.

blocks.caption: As it forages, a bee carries pollen from flower to flower

blocks.text: A single bee can visit up to 700 flowers in one day. To produce just 500 grams of honey, a whole colony has to fly the equivalent of three times around the Earth.

About **75% of the world's food crops** depend, at least a little, on pollinators such as bees. That includes coffee, cocoa, apples, almonds and avocados. Pollination's contribution to the world economy is estimated at between 235 and 577 billion dollars a year.

sections.title: Pollination, quiet work that is essential

blocks.text: The decline of bees has no single cause: several threats act at the same time. Since the 1990s, some beekeepers have lost 30% to 50% of their colonies each winter, when natural losses should be around 10%. This sudden vanishing is sometimes called [[colony collapse disorder]].

blocks.caption: Neonicotinoids spread through the whole plant, including nectar and pollen

blocks.text: [[Neonicotinoids]], a family of insecticides, are especially to blame. They soak into the entire plant, including its nectar and its pollen. Even in small doses they disorient bees, which can no longer find their hive, and they weaken the insects' immune systems.

On top of that come a parasitic mite that carries deadly viruses, the loss of wild flowers to monoculture farming, and climate change, which shifts flowering times out of step with the moment insects wake up.

When we say “bee,” we almost always picture the honeybee, the one that lives in a hive and makes honey. Yet it is only one species among more than **20,000** worldwide, alongside bumblebees and mason bees. Most are solitary and make no honey, but their ecological role is just as important.
Some flowers, tomato blossoms among them, release their pollen only under a precise vibration. Honeybees cannot do it, but bumblebees can, thanks to a technique called sonication.

These wild species are often specialized on one particular plant, and are sometimes the only ones able to pollinate it well. They are also more vulnerable than the honeybee, since nobody monitors or cares for them. Their disappearance weakens the whole [[food chain]], because many birds depend on the fruits and seeds that pollination produces.

sections.title: There is more than one kind of bee

blocks.text: Cutting pesticide use remains the most effective lever. In 2018 the European Union banned three major neonicotinoids in open fields. Alongside that, restoring [[agroecological infrastructures]], such as hedges or strips of wildflowers, recreates refuges for insects.
Anyone can act in simple ways: planting local flowers in a garden, or letting the lawn grow a little longer before mowing, offers bees a real refuge when flowers are scarce.
Protecting pollinators is not only about saving nature. It is a long-term survival strategy, because their work directly supports the ability of plants to feed us.

Bees and the 20,000 species of wild pollinators make reproduction possible for 75% of the world's food crops. Their decline, driven by pesticides, parasites and habitat loss, is a direct threat to our food.

subtitle: The small workers behind our food
title: Why are bees vital?
